title: Admin telemetry extraction & retention sync - Cascade Financial
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC2 & ISO artifact links by 2025-06-19
SE to run sample audit export to customer's S3 by 2025-06-23
Customer to confirm retention policy target (90 vs 365 days) by 2025-06-20
action_items: Liam O'Connor: Share export schema and sample payloads (by 2025-06-18)
Maya Chen: Send SOC2 Type II summary and contact for compliance pack (by 2025-06-19)
Tom Alvarez: Provide S3 bucket ARN and test creds for export (by 2025-06-23)
header: Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Ravi Desai (Redwood CSM); Priya Rao (Cascade Head of Security), Tom Alvarez (Cascade Cloud Eng), Elena Martins (Cascade Compliance), Marcus Bell (Cascade SRE)
summary: Focused review of Redwood's admin activity and audit telemetry: what events are captured, export delivery options (S3, BigQuery, webhook), log schema, retention controls, and how this maps to Cascade Financial's SOC2/ISO requirements. Agreed next steps: share artifacts, run a sample export, and decide on retention window.
topics: What admin activity is logged (logins, API keys, role changes, model deploys, dataset access)
Export mechanisms: batch S3 export, streaming webhook, Pub/Sub/BigQuery sinks
Retention windows and legal hold / exportable archives
KMS / key rotation and how encrypted logs are stored
Private/VPC deployment nuances and on-prem audit forwarding
transcript: [00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. We wanted to walk through the admin telemetry story end-to-end so you can validate it against Cascade's controls.

[00:00:12] Priya Rao: Thanks Maya. High level — we need to confirm that changes to admin roles, API tokens, model rollouts, and access to sensitive datasets are captured and exportable. SOC 2 says we need immutable audit trails for those actions.

[00:00:28] Liam O'Connor: Totally. Quick overview: Redwood captures user-level events (login, logout, MFA failures), token and key lifecycle events (create, rotate, revoke), RBAC changes (role assign/remove), and platform operations like model deploys, rollback, and endpoint configuration changes. We also log system-level events such as node restarts and autoscale triggers, but those are tagged separately.
[00:00:50] Marcus Bell: Can you clarify how model deploys are recorded? Is it the commit ID, the operator, and timestamp? We need enough context to tie a deploy to a person for audit trails.

[00:01:05] Liam O'Connor: Yes — each deploy event includes actor (username or service account), deployment id, model version, commit/tag, region, and a small payload with pre/post config diffs. There is a KV 'cash' — sorry KV cache — identifier if caching is involved, and the artifact digest. Sometimes transcripts show 'KV cash' in our notes, it's just a common ASR quirk.
[00:01:28] Elena Martins: How are admin console interactions captured? For example, if someone edits a rollout policy through the UI vs via API, does that matter?

[00:01:39] Liam O'Connor: We capture both. Source is annotated (UI / API / CLI / automation). The audit record has a source field and any attached metadata. UI edits also include session id and IP address when available, subject to privacy rules.
[00:01:50] Tom Alvarez: About export options — we need to pipe logs into our long-term store. What sinks do you support out of the box?

[00:02:00] Maya Chen: Right now Redwood supports scheduled batch exports to S3 (parquet or JSONL), streaming webhooks for near real-time, and direct sinks to BigQuery and Kafka. We can also do one-off exports for compliance requests.
[00:02:14] Priya Rao: Does S3 export support server-side encryption with our KMS? We require that artifacts are encrypted with our key.

[00:02:24] Liam O'Connor: Yes. For hosted deployments we support SSE-KMS where we use customer-managed keys via AWS KMS — you can provide an ARN. For Private/VPC deployments you manage keys on premise or via your cloud KMS; logs written to your S3 are encrypted with your key. We also have options to encrypt fields in the payload at the application layer.
[00:02:40] Priya Rao: And what about rotation? If we rotate the KMS key, does the past archive remain decryptable?

[00:02:48] Liam O'Connor: As long as you keep the old key policy and keys in AWS KMS (or continue to allow decryption), yes. If you permanently schedule key deletion you'll need to export plaintext before that. We can provide guidance on key rotation best practices.
[00:02:58] Elena Martins: Can we do immutable write-once exports? For compliance we prefer S3 with object lock/Governance mode.

[00:03:07] Maya Chen: We can write to your S3 bucket and you can enable object lock/Governance there. Redwood doesn't enforce object lock from our side for hosted S3 destinations, but for Private deployments we can integrate with your storage policies to ensure immutability.
[00:03:20] Tom Alvarez: Schema — can you share sample payloads? Our legal team needs to know which fields are present so they index correctly.

[00:03:28] Liam O'Connor: Absolutely. I'll share a sample export schema and a few redacted examples. The schema includes event_id, timestamp, actor, actor_type, action, resource_type, resource_id, change_summary, source, user_ip, request_id, and related_trace_id. There are also optional fields for model_version and kv_cache_keys — again, ASR sometimes writes kv_cash but it's kv_cache.
[00:03:48] Priya Rao: What about PII? We have to avoid storing full usernames in exported logs for some jurisdictions. Can you redact or hash certain fields?

[00:03:58] Liam O'Connor: Yes. We support on-export transformations: you can request hashing of username/email, or we can exclude some fields. For hosted logs, we have at-rest retention rules; for exports we push the exact payload you request to your sink — so do the PII handling on your side or request that Redwood redact before export.
[00:04:14] Priya Rao: Data residency — our policy requires logs for EU customers to stay in EU regions. How do you handle region scoping for exports?

[00:04:23] Maya Chen: Redwood's smart routing can pin audit exports to a region. For Hosted customers we keep region-scoped exports in the same region as the tenant. For Dedicated or Private, you control the storage endpoint.
[00:04:33] Marcus Bell: Is the audit log chain tamper-evident? We need to show integrity for an external audit.

[00:04:40] Liam O'Connor: We generate checksums per-file and maintain a write sequence number. For higher assurance we can append a cryptographic HMAC signing step on export using a key you provide; that way you can verify immutability independently.
[00:04:53] Elena Martins: How long do you retain logs in the platform before export? We may want a 90 day hot window and 7 year cold archive.

[00:05:02] Maya Chen: By default Redwood retains admin audit events for 90 days in the platform. You can configure retention for Dedicated customers up to 365 days, and with Private deployments we can meet multi-year retention when you supply storage. For long-term archiving we recommend exporting to your S3/BigQuery and applying your lifecycle rules to get to 7 years.
[00:05:18] Tom Alvarez: If we enable automatic export every 24h, does it export deltas or full dump? We want to minimize egress and duplication.

[00:05:26] Liam O'Connor: Exports support incremental mode (only new events since last successful export) and full snapshots. Incremental is the default for daily jobs and uses event sequence markers to ensure idempotency.
[00:05:36] Priya Rao: For legal hold, can we pause deletion even if retention window passes?

[00:05:42] Maya Chen: Yes — we support a hold flag at the tenant or object level. For hosted customers you request a legal hold and we suspend automatic lifecycle deletion. For Dedicated/Private you control lifecycle in your storage.
[00:05:52] Marcus Bell: Regarding SSO, when a user authenticates through SAML/SSO, do you log the identity provider's assertion id? We need to map SAML session to events.

[00:06:00] Liam O'Connor: We include SSO provider metadata: assertion id, IdP entity id, and the nameID used. We also capture SAML attribute mappings when present. Note that sometimes attributes are missing — we annotate that in the event.
[00:06:12] Elena Martins: Do you support per-route RBAC audit reports? For instance, we want a filtered feed of only role-change and key-rotation events.

[00:06:20] Liam O'Connor: Yes, export filters let you pick event types, actor groups, and resource scopes. You can define a subscription that only sends role-change and key lifecycle events to a separate webhook or S3 prefix.
[00:06:31] Tom Alvarez: On the transport security side, webhooks are delivered over TLS with client certs, right? We need mutual TLS for ingestion.
[00:06:38] Maya Chen: We support mTLS for webhook deliveries, signed payloads via HMAC, and likewise are happy to set up a private peering path for high-volume customers.
[00:06:48] Priya Rao: A quick question on logs for system-level operators: do you record automated system actions separately so we can exclude noisy autoscale events from compliance reports?

[00:06:56] Liam O'Connor: Yes — system actions are labeled actor_type: system and can be filtered out. We also provide sampling controls for high-volume system events so they don't blow up your storage.
[00:07:06] Marcus Bell: If we have a Private deployment on-prem, can you still push Red-wood managed control plane logs to our SIEM? We prefer the control plane events locally.

[00:07:14] Liam O'Connor: For Private, the control plane can be configured to push directly to your SIEM (Splunk/QRadar) over secure channels. If you need, we can run a forwarder container inside your network to avoid exfiltration.
[00:07:24] Elena Martins: Regarding SOC 2 artifacts — can you share the scope mapping: which audit logs map to CC6/CC7 controls?
[00:07:31] Maya Chen: Yes, Maya: action item — I'll send a mapping doc. We also have a one-pager in the compliance pack that shows which events map to common SOC2 criteria and ISO 27001 controls.
[00:07:40] Priya Rao: What about alerts and regressions? If a key rotation fails we want an immediate notification plus audit entry.
[00:07:47] Liam O'Connor: Failures emit an alert event and we can hook that into your PagerDuty or webhook. The audit record includes error codes and retry attempts.
[00:07:56] Tom Alvarez: About queryability — once exported to BigQuery, is the schema stable or do you add fields over time?
[00:08:03] Liam O'Connor: We try to keep the core schema stable. Additions are appendix fields and we version the schema. Exports include a schema_version and changelog so you can handle migrations.
[00:08:14] Priya Rao: Can you red-team the audit pipeline? We want assurance that a compromised account can't just delete or alter logs and cover tracks.

[00:08:23] Maya Chen: We offer an integrity review as part of our enterprise onboarding where our security team will walk your auditors through the pipeline. For hosted customers, deletion APIs are restricted and require privileged approval; we also have an immutable backup export option.
[00:08:34] Marcus Bell: One edge case — machine-to-machine tokens created by CI systems: do you attribute the human who rotated them or just the service account?

[00:08:42] Liam O'Connor: We capture both if the rotation was performed by a user-mediated action. For automated rotations triggered by CI, we include the automation user/service account and link to the request_id. You can decide to require justification metadata during rotation for better traceability.
[00:08:55] Tom Alvarez: Is there a sandbox we can use to validate the export before we plug our production bucket?
[00:09:02] Maya Chen: Yes — we can spin up a sandbox tenant with synthetic events and run an export job against your test bucket. Liam, that's an action for you to set up the sample job.
[00:09:08] Liam O'Connor: Yep. I'll set up daily incremental exports to the test S3 you provide and share the schema and sample files.
[00:09:14] Priya Rao: A minor point — how do you handle GDPR DSARs that reference audit logs? If a user asks for records about them, can we extract a user-focused subset?

[00:09:23] Liam O'Connor: We support subject-focused exports: filter by actor or resource and generate a user bundle including activity and session metadata. There is a retention and redaction workflow if needed.
[00:09:33] Elena Martins: For our internal auditors, can you provide a short-runbook of how to verify the chain of custody for an exported file?

[00:09:39] Maya Chen: Yes — runbook is in our compliance pack. I'll attach it. Also I'll include the link to our API docs for audit export: https://dash.redwood.ai/docs/audit-exports (note: link in transcript may be slightly different in the portal).
[00:09:55] Tom Alvarez: There was earlier mention of HSM — how does Redwood integrate with Cloud HSM or on-prem HSM for key signing of audit bundles?

[00:10:03] Liam O'Connor: We can sign bundles using keys in CloudHSM or a customer HSM for Private installs. For hosted customers, we have a managed signing option but can also accept signatures produced externally.
[00:10:12] Priya Rao: Let's talk retention decisioning. Our default preference is 365 days for hot logs, and anything older should be in immutable cold archive for 7 years. Is that feasible?

[00:10:22] Maya Chen: That is feasible under Dedicated or Private. For Hosted we can do 365 days for enterprise tiers but for multi-year you should export to your storage and apply lifecycle for 7 years.
[00:10:31] Priya Rao: Good. Any gotchas with indexing or costs? We need an estimate of egress.

[00:10:36] Liam O'Connor: Egress depends on volume. We typically provide a model: events per user per day * avg bytes per event to estimate monthly egress. We'll run an estimate after we see your event rate sample. Incremental exports cut down duplicates.
[00:10:47] Marcus Bell: One more technical: request tracing — do you include trace ids so we can stitch audit events back to logs and traces in our APM?
[00:10:55] Liam O'Connor: Yes, events include request_id and related_trace_id which map to our distributed tracing. We can also emit observability hooks to your tracing system if needed.

[00:11:04] Maya Chen: Okay, let's recap and assign next steps. Liam will share schema and sample payloads; I'll send SOC2/ISO summary and the compliance runbook; Tom will provide the test S3 ARN. We agreed to a sandbox export by 2025-06-23.
[00:11:20] Priya Rao: Sounds good. Also, please include a short note about how to handle legal holds and emergency data access requests.
[00:11:27] Maya Chen: Will do. Anything else?
[00:11:31] Tom Alvarez: No, that's it from me. Thanks everyone.
[00:11:34] Elena Martins: Thank you. We'll review the artifacts when they arrive and confirm retention choice.
[00:11:38] Maya Chen: Great, we'll follow up via the CRM and I will attach the docs in the Hub. End of call.
